issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies imply a current external danger/assault-style threat context (arming oneself, hypervigilant scanning for physical threat) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is usually medical and not mitigated by carrying a weapon or scanning for attackers.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Within the profile, these threat-focused safety behaviours are not supported by any Threat items and fit poorly with the formulation, which has Triggers and Threat fully inactive; they suggest a strong trigger/threat loop that the rest of the self-report does not reflect.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. It is more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral injury and lacks support from the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding medical cues is plausible for a child's severe illness, but the additional strategies of avoiding public transport and constantly scanning for external threat suggest a danger-based trauma context not represented in the memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: For trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, avoiding public transport is hard to link clinically unless other items indicate transport-related reminders or hospital-travel cues; no such trigger or memory content is present here, so this strategy appears context-mismatched.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Constantly scanning the environment for threat implies an ongoing external danger focus, but the rest of the profile is dominated by trauma-memory disorganisation and self-change appraisals rather than current external-threat concerns. With Threat and Trigger links inactive, this item sits awkwardly in the formulation.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) and the rest of the profile. The selected appraisals and memory items center on traumatic recollection, permanent change, and distrust, but not on a current external danger context. 'Constantly scan environment for signs of threat' implies hypervigilance for immediate environmental threat, which is more characteristic of assault/combat-type trauma and is not clinically linked here given that all Triggers and Threat edges are inactive in the formulation. It also sits poorly with the other maladaptive strategies, which are illness/trauma-processing related (avoid care, suppress thoughts).

vignette: Mr. Arun Patel, a 69‑year‑old South‑Eastern Asian widower, had spent most of his adult life caring for children in families across the city. In the summer of 2013, a small, bright‑eyed boy named Dev, whom Arun had been nannying, was brought to the hospital with an unrelenting fever and a rash that spread across his arms. The diagnosis, announced with a hushed urgency, was aplastic anemia, a life‑threatening condition that would require months of intensive care and chemotherapy. Arun watched his little charge lie pale and sweating, his own heart pounding in his ears. The memory of that day is not a single, coherent narrative; instead, it is a collage of fragments: the sound of Dev’s labored breathing, the fluorescent light flickering overhead, the sharp scent of antiseptic, and the feeling of helplessness that flooded Arun’s chest. To him, those fragments are more vivid than any ordinary memory, and they do not sit neatly in the past—they feel as if they are happening again whenever he thinks of the boy’s fever. Because the recollections are so present and unfiltered, Arun came to see himself as “unrecognisable to me.” The man who once laughed at children’s jokes now feels alien, his sense of identity fractured. The conviction that he has been “permanently damaged for the worse” grows with each recall of Dev’s suffering. Arun also began to distrust others, believing that people’s words might hide hidden agendas and that medical staff could be indifferent to the suffering of a child. These negative appraisals shape the way Arun engages with the world and, in particular, the ways he copes with the memory of the event. Arun’s negative beliefs about himself and others immediately led him to adopt a set of maladaptive strategies. He stopped seeking routine medical care, convinced that doctors would not understand his pain or that any visit might remind him of the boy’s illness. He actively suppressed thoughts of the incident, telling himself that the only way to survive was to ignore the trauma. When he could not suppress the images, he filled his mind with other stimuli—watching television, reading about sports, or scrolling through social media—so that he could “keep his mind occupied all the time.” Each avoidance, each distraction, only reinforced his belief that he had been irrevocably altered. The same negative beliefs that guided Arun’s avoidance also altered how he re‑experiences the memory itself. He began to interpret the vivid recollections as proof that the trauma had changed him forever. Because he believed the event was permanently damaging, he could not process the incident in a linear, coherent story; instead, he kept the memory fragmented and stuck in the present. The fragmented memory, in turn, perpetuates his negative appraisal that he has become an unrecognisable, damaged man. When Arun’s memory continues to feel present and overwhelmingly real, it prompts him to further engage in maladaptive strategies. The distressing images compel him to suppress any thoughts about the boy’s illness; each attempt at suppression is accompanied by a desperate urge to distract himself. In the kitchen of the family home he nurses, he might rush to the fridge, pull out a bag of chips, and eat in silence while the memory of Dev’s fever flickers in his mind. By suppressing the memory, Arun temporarily eases the emotional turmoil, but the act of suppression strengthens the memory’s vividness, keeping it at the forefront of his consciousness. Because Arun’s avoidance of medical appointments, his mental distraction, and his relentless suppression of the trauma all reinforce the intensity and immediacy of the memory, a self‑reinforcing cycle has emerged. The memory remains more real than normal, it feels present, and it continuously fuels Arun’s belief that he has become a damaged, unrecognisable man who cannot trust others. These thoughts, in turn, drive him to avoid medical care, to suppress the memory, and to keep his mind constantly busy. The loop tightens as the months pass, and Arun’s reluctance to confront the past deepens his sense of isolation and disconnection from his own identity. After years of living with this invisible burden, Arun finally sought help. The day he decided to schedule an appointment with a therapist was triggered by an overheard conversation in the school cafeteria: a teacher lamented the lack of support for children dealing with chronic illness, and the words echoed the unresolved fear Arun has carried for years. He is now fearful that confronting the memory might shatter the fragile identity he has built around being a caretaker, but he also hopes that acknowledging the trauma will allow him to reclaim a sense of self and to end the cycle of avoidance that has isolated him from his own family and from his work.
